unit.title: Earth and its habitats
unit.blurb: Inside the Earth, volcanoes, earthquakes, and the many habitats where plants and animals live.

O1.t: Know that the Earth has layers: crust, mantle and core.

O2.t: Know what a volcano is, and the difference between magma and lava.

O3.t: Know that earthquakes happen when plates of the crust move, and how to stay safe.

O4.t: Know that a habitat gives a living thing food, water and shelter, and name some habitats.

captions: Hello, Earth explorers!
What is inside our planet? Let's dig down!
This is lesson 4.1: the structure of the Earth.
Think about a peach.
It has a thin skin on the outside.
Under the skin is soft fruit.
And in the centre is a hard stone. The Earth has layers, a bit like a peach!
The Earth has three main layers.
We live on the crust. It is the thin, rocky outside.
Under the crust is the mantle. It is very hot rock that moves slowly.
In the middle is the core. It is the hottest part of all!
Pause and think.
Which layer of the Earth do we live on?
Imagine a journey down into the Earth.
Your house sits on the crust.
As we dig down, the rocks get hotter and hotter.
The mantle is hot rock. And the core is as hot as the surface of the Sun!
Did you know?
Nobody has ever dug through the crust.
The deepest hole ever dug is about twelve kilometres deep. The Earth is much, much bigger!
Riddle time!
What has a core, but is not an apple?
The Earth!
Your turn.
Which layer is in the very middle of the Earth?
Let's make a play-dough Earth.
Make a small red ball for the core, and cover it in orange for the mantle.
Add a thin brown layer for the crust.
Ask an adult to cut it in half. Can you see the layers?
Let's remember.
The Earth has layers.
We live on the thin, rocky crust.
The mantle is very hot rock.
And the core, in the middle, is the hottest part. Down-to-earth work!

captions: Hello, Earth explorers!
Get ready for something hot and loud!
This is lesson 4.2: volcanoes.
Look at this quiet mountain.
Deep inside, hot melted rock is pushing up.
Rumble, rumble… boom! The volcano erupts!
Red hot lava flows down the side.
Melted rock inside the Earth is called magma.
When it comes out of a volcano, we call it lava.
Volcanoes can also blow out ash and smoke.
Pause and think.
What do we call melted rock that comes out of a volcano?
Some people live near volcanoes.
Volcano soil is very good for growing food.
Scientists watch volcanoes carefully.
If a volcano might erupt, people move to a safe place.
Did you know?
Lava is super hot.
It can be ten times hotter than boiling water!
Joke time!
What did one volcano say to the other volcano?
I lava you!
Your turn.
Why do some farmers like to live near volcanoes?
Let's make a model volcano. Ask an adult to help.
Build sand around a small bottle, like a mountain.
Put baking soda inside the bottle.
Pour in some vinegar, and watch it erupt!
Let's remember.
A volcano is where melted rock comes out of the Earth.
Inside the Earth, melted rock is called magma.
Outside, it is called lava.
And volcano soil is great for farming. Explosive work!

captions: Hello, Earth explorers!
Sometimes the ground starts to shake.
This is lesson 4.3: earthquakes.
Imagine a quiet town.
Suddenly, the ground starts to shake!
Cups rattle and pictures fall off the wall.
This is an earthquake.
The Earth's crust is broken into huge pieces, called plates.
The plates move very, very slowly.
Sometimes they get stuck, then slip suddenly. Jolt! That makes an earthquake.
Pause and think.
What are the big pieces of the Earth's crust called?
Do you know what to do in an earthquake?
Drop down to the floor.
Cover your head, under a strong table.
Hold on, until the shaking stops. Drop, cover and hold on!
Did you know?
Some tall buildings are built to sway gently, like a tree in the wind.
That helps them stay standing in an earthquake!
Joke time!
What did the ground say during the earthquake?
Sorry, I am a bit shaky today!
Your turn.
What should you do first in an earthquake?
Let's test some towers.
Build a tall, thin tower of blocks on a tray, and shake the tray gently.
Now build a wide tower, and shake again.
Which tower stayed up better?
Let's remember.
In an earthquake, the ground shakes.
The Earth's crust is broken into plates.
When the plates slip suddenly, the ground shakes.
And to stay safe: drop, cover and hold on! Rock-solid work!

captions: Hello, nature explorers!
Animals and plants live in many different places.
This is lesson 4.4: different habitats.
Every living thing has a home, called its habitat.
A camel lives in the hot, dry desert.
A polar bear lives in the icy Arctic. A fish lives in the ocean.
And a monkey lives in the warm, wet rainforest.
Pause and think.
What is a habitat?
A good habitat gives animals what they need.
It gives them food.
It gives them water.
And it gives them shelter, a safe place to rest.
There are habitats near your home too!
A tree is a habitat for birds and insects.
Under a stone, you might find woodlice.
And a pond is a habitat for frogs and fish.
Did you know?
Rainforests cover only a small part of the Earth.
But more than half of all kinds of animals and plants live there!
Joke time!
What animal is always at a game of cricket?
A bat!
Your turn.
Which animal's habitat is the hot desert?
Let's go on a minibeast hunt, with an adult.
Look gently under stones and leaves.
Draw the minibeasts you find.
Then put everything back, so their habitat stays safe.
Let's remember.
A habitat is where a plant or animal lives.
A habitat gives food, water and shelter.
Deserts, oceans and rainforests are habitats.
And there are small habitats near your home too. Wild work!
